author: Peter L. Bernstein
biz: Separate your risk from your uncertainty

Split this month's marketing decisions into two lists. Risk is a channel with enough history to carry an honest base rate, where a cost per funded case means something. Uncertainty is a new creative, a new keyword set or a changed regulatory landscape, where the past number is decoration. Fund the first from measured performance. Fund the second as a deliberately small experiment sized so that being wrong costs you nothing you need. This week, tag every live campaign as risk or uncertainty, and measure cost per funded case only on the first group, with a minimum volume before you act.
Price the downside for the actual person

Bernoulli's point is a Consumer Duty point. The same monthly payment is an inconvenience for one borrower and the beginning of real trouble for another, so a recommendation that is fine on average can be poor for the person in front of you. This week, add one line to the Debt Support Direct and broker files: what specifically happens to this client if their income drops for three months. Measure the share of files that carry a recorded answer, and review any case where the answer is severe before it progresses.
book: Against the Gods: The Remarkable Story of Risk

b: Peter Lewyn Bernstein was born in New York on the twenty second of January 1919, into a family that had made its money in leather. He went to the Ethical Culture School, where in his first year of lessons he sat beside a boy called Robert Heilbroner, who would grow up to write one of the most read histories of economic thought there has ever been. The two of them stayed friends for the next seventy years.

In 1929, when Peter was ten, his father Allen sold the leather factory. It was a good price and a sensible age to stop, and Allen took the proceeds of a lifetime of work and put them into the stock market, which had been rising for most of the decade and showed every sign of carrying on.

Then came October. The crash took most of what the family had. Nobody in the house had been reckless. His father had read the papers, taken advice, done what careful men were doing. The money went anyway.

A boy learns something from that which no lecture can teach him. Not that markets are wicked, and not that his father was a fool, but something stranger and harder to hold on to: that a reasonable decision and a terrible outcome can be the same decision. Seventy years later Bernstein would still be telling investors to treat their gains as a loan the market could call in without notice. He had watched the loan called in once, from the hallway.

b: He went on to Horace Mann, then to Harvard, where he read economics and graduated in 1940, magna cum laude and Phi Beta Kappa, in a class that also contained John Kennedy. It was an odd moment to study the subject. The Depression was still on, the old certainties had failed in public, and the men teaching him were arguing about why.
In 1941 he joined the research staff of the Federal Reserve Bank of New York. He was twenty two, sitting among people whose job was to measure an economy that nobody had successfully predicted.

Underneath all of it sat a question he would spend his life circling, and would finally write a whole book to answer. Why did it take humanity so long to learn to measure uncertainty at all? The Greeks had geometry and logic. The Romans built roads across a continent. Both gambled constantly. Neither worked out the odds.

Bernstein's answer, when it came, was that something genuinely new had happened in Europe, and that we underrate how new it was. His opening line is one of the great opening lines of modern non fiction. The revolutionary idea that defines the boundary between modern times and the past, he wrote, is the mastery of risk: the notion that the future is more than a whim of the gods. Before that idea, the future was weather. After it, the future was a problem.

b: After Pearl Harbor he joined up. His eyesight was too poor for a cockpit, so he was sent instead to the Office of Strategic Services, the American wartime intelligence service, and posted to London. He spent the bombing there. He said afterwards that London taught him how to keep thinking while frightened, which is a skill most people assume they have and very few actually do.

It is worth pausing on what a man in London in 1943 could and could not know. He could know roughly how many bombers came on an average night, and roughly how many houses burned. He could not know whether his own street was next. The two kinds of ignorance are completely different, and almost everyone muddles them.

This is the hinge of the whole book. The word risk comes to us from the early Italian risicare, which means to dare. Bernstein loved that, because of what it implies. Risk, he wrote, is a choice rather than a fate. The gambler at the table is not suffering something. He is doing something.

Fate you endure. Risk you choose, and having chosen it, you can study it, price it, spread it, hedge it or walk away from it. That shift, from weather to choice, is the thing the ancients never made, and the thing a handful of Europeans made over about three hundred years.
ch.cap: Thinking clearly while the bombs fall

b: The war ended and Bernstein taught economics at Williams College in Massachusetts, then spent several years in banking. In 1951, after his father died, the family insisted he take over the investment firm his father had founded with Frederick Macaulay, the economist who had worked out how to measure a bond's sensitivity to interest rates. So the son went into the business of handling other people's uncertainty for a living, which is one way to describe money management and the most honest way.

The history he would later tell begins with a merchant's son. In 1202 Leonardo of Pisa, whom we call Fibonacci, published Liber Abaci, and brought the Hindu Arabic numerals properly into European commerce. It sounds like a footnote. It is not. You cannot calculate an expectation in Roman numerals. The arithmetic of risk needed a notation first.

Then in 1494 a Franciscan friar called Luca Pacioli, the man who codified double entry bookkeeping, set a puzzle. Two players are partway through a game of chance and must stop. How should the stake be divided? It is a question about a future that will now never happen, and for nearly two centuries nobody could answer it.

The first man who came close was Girolamo Cardano, a sixteenth century physician, mathematician and compulsive gambler, who wrote a short book on games of chance that contains the beginnings of probability. He never published it. It appeared in 1663, nearly a century after his death, by which time others had got there without him.

b: The breakthrough came in letters. In the summer of 1654 a French gambler and man of letters, the Chevalier de Mere, put Pacioli's unfinished game to Blaise Pascal. Pascal wrote to Pierre de Fermat, a lawyer in Toulouse and one of the finest mathematicians alive, and over a handful of letters the two of them solved it.

Their answer was not simply arithmetic. They worked out that the stake should be split according to each player's chance of winning from where the game stood, which meant assigning a number to something that had not happened. That is the invention. Not the odds of a dice roll, which gamblers had always felt in their bones, but the idea that a possible future can carry a measurable value today.

Everything we now do with money descends from those letters. An insurance premium is a number attached to a fire that has not happened. A share price is a number attached to profits nobody has earned yet. A lender's interest rate is a number attached to a default that may never come.

Pascal then did something stranger. Having invented a way to weigh uncertain outcomes, he applied it to God, and argued that given an infinite prize and a finite stake, belief is the rational wager. You may think it a poor argument about religion. As a piece of decision making it is startling. It is the first time anyone reasons formally about what to do when you cannot know, rather than about what is true.
ch.cap: Two mathematicians invent the future's price

b: The next step was taken by a shopkeeper. John Graunt sold buttons and ribbons in London, and in 1662 he published a small book based on the Bills of Mortality, the weekly parish lists of who had died and of what. From a heap of clerical scribble he produced the first serious table of human life expectancy, and something else besides: he showed you could learn about a whole population from a sample of it.

Thirty years later the astronomer Edmond Halley, the man with the comet, was given the records of the city of Breslau, which kept unusually careful registers of births and deaths. In 1693 he turned them into a proper mortality table and showed how to price a life annuity honestly, by age. Governments had been selling annuities for years at a flat price regardless of the buyer's age, which is a lovely deal if you are young and a disaster for the treasury.

That is the moment risk becomes an industry. Within a generation the coffee house of a man named Edward Lloyd was the place where shipowners and underwriters met, and marine insurance became a trade. Pooling was the trick. No one could say which ship would sink. Everyone could say roughly how many would.

Bernstein was running portfolios while he thought about this. Diversification, he knew, is Graunt and Halley wearing a suit. You cannot know which holding fails. You can arrange your affairs so that one failing does not finish you.

b: In 1713, eight years after his death, Jacob Bernoulli's Ars Conjectandi appeared, and with it the law of large numbers: as you take more observations, the measured frequency closes in on the true one. Bernoulli was careful about the limits of this. Nature's urn, he pointed out, is not a real urn. We do not know how many balls it holds or of what colours, and we can only reason backwards from what we have drawn.

Then in 1738 his nephew Daniel Bernoulli published something that reads like modern behavioural economics two and a half centuries early. Offered a gamble with an infinite mathematical expectation, nobody will pay much for a ticket. The reason, Daniel said, is that we do not value money, we value what money does for us, and the thousandth pound matters less to a rich man than the first pound matters to a poor one.

That single move changes the subject. Risk stops being a property of the dice and becomes a relationship between the dice and the person holding them. The same bet is prudent for one man and reckless for his neighbour.

Around them the machinery was being built: Abraham de Moivre, a Huguenot refugee doing mathematics in a London coffee house, describing in 1733 the bell shaped curve and how observations scatter around an average, and Thomas Bayes, a Presbyterian minister whose essay appeared in 1763 after his death, showing how a belief should be revised in the light of new evidence. Between them they gave us the normal distribution and the habit of updating.

b: Francis Galton was a Victorian gentleman of restless curiosity and some deeply unpleasant opinions about heredity. In 1875 he planted sweet peas of carefully graded sizes and measured their offspring, and in a paper of the following decade on human height he described what he found: the children of very tall parents tend to be tall, but less tall. Extremes pull back towards the middle. He called it regression.

For anyone who handles money this is the most useful idea in the book, and the most dangerous. It tells you that the brilliant fund manager was partly lucky and that the dreadful year is probably not the new normal. It does not tell you when the pull back will happen, or how far past the mean the swing will go first. Bernstein's warning is exact: regression is a tendency, not a timetable, and men have been ruined waiting for it.

His own working life ran through those swings. The family firm was sold in 1967. In 1973 he resigned and set up on his own as a consultant to institutions. In 1974, in the middle of the worst bear market since the war, with portfolios cut in half and nobody in any mood for theory, he founded the Journal of Portfolio Management.

That timing was deliberate. The academic work on risk was piling up unread in universities while practitioners lost fortunes without it. He spent the rest of his life carrying ideas across that gap in both directions.

b: In 1921 two books appeared that said the same awkward thing. Frank Knight, in Chicago, published Risk, Uncertainty and Profit. John Maynard Keynes, in Cambridge, published A Treatise on Probability. Both insisted on a distinction that the next eighty years of finance would repeatedly forget.

Risk, in Knight's sense, is the kind of unknown you can put a number on, because you know the shape of the possibilities. Uncertainty is the kind you cannot, because the situation is genuinely new. The chance of a fire in a city of a million houses is risk. The chance of this particular war, this particular technology, this particular panic, is uncertainty. Keynes put it with his usual bluntness: about such matters, there is no scientific basis on which to form any calculable probability whatever. We simply do not know.

The machinery got built anyway, and it was magnificent. In 1944 John von Neumann and Oskar Morgenstern published the theory of games, putting rational choice under uncertainty on a formal footing. In 1952 a graduate student called Harry Markowitz published a fourteen page paper, Portfolio Selection, which showed mathematically what your grandmother knew: that the risk of a portfolio is not the sum of the risks of its holdings, because they do not all move together. Diversification became something you could calculate.

Then in 1973 Fischer Black, Myron Scholes and Robert Merton gave the world a formula for pricing an option, and an industry of derivatives grew up on it. Risk could now be sliced, priced and sold to whoever wanted it. All of it rested on a single assumption, politely buried in the mathematics: that the future would scatter about the way the past had.
ch.cap: Measurable risk is not real uncertainty

b: The last turn of the book is the sharpest. In 1979 two Israeli psychologists, Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky, published prospect theory, and demonstrated that the person at the centre of all this elegant machinery does not behave as the machinery assumes. We feel a loss far more than an equivalent gain. We answer the same question differently depending on whether it is put to us in terms of survival or death. We are not bad calculators so much as inconsistent ones.

Bernstein wrote Against the Gods in his seventies, and it was published in 1996. He was not writing to debunk the models. He had spent his career defending them against people who preferred hunches. But he ended the book on a warning, and the warning is the reason it has lasted. The models work by assuming the future resembles the past. When it does not, they fail precisely when you need them, and the more faith we place in the numbers, the larger the failure.

He lived to watch it happen twice. In 1998 a hedge fund staffed with Nobel laureates lost most of its capital in weeks when Russian debt behaved in a way the model had priced as essentially impossible. In 2008 the whole system did it at once.

He kept changing his mind in public, which is rare at any age. In 2003, at eighty four, he argued that the fixed long term asset allocation he had helped make orthodox was no longer good enough. Asked what mattered most, he said the hardest thing to unlearn is the belief that you can work out the future. Being wrong, he said, is part of the process.

Peter Bernstein died on the fifth of June 2009, aged ninety, as the crisis he had spent a lifetime describing was still running. The question he had been asking since 1970 is the one worth keeping. Not what will happen. What are the consequences if I am wrong?

connects: Bernstein's final chapter rests on the prospect theory work that Kahneman tells from the inside, that the people using risk models are not the consistent calculators the models assume.
Taleb's black swan is precisely the wildness Bernstein's last pages warn is waiting outside every distribution built from the past.
Fortune's Formula is the practical descendant of Daniel Bernoulli's utility: not whether a bet is favourable, but how much of what you already have to stake on it.
note: Built from Bernstein's Against the Gods, published by Wiley in 1996, and from the detailed obituaries and interviews that followed his death in June 2009, including Jason Zweig's memoir of him. The 1929 episode, his OSS posting to London, the 1951 takeover of Bernstein-Macaulay and the founding of the Journal of Portfolio Management in 1974 are all documented. The famous story that Charles II told the Royal Society to admit Graunt and any other such tradesman without further fuss is widely repeated but hard to verify in that exact form, so treat it as a good story rather than a quotation. Later events challenged the book's tradition more than the book itself: the collapses of 1998 and 2008 showed the quantitative risk machinery failing in precisely the way Bernstein's final chapter warned it would, and critics such as Nassim Taleb argued he was still too generous to it.
recall: What did Pascal and Fermat actually solve in 1654, and why did it matter?

They solved the problem of the points: how to divide the stake of a game of chance abandoned before the end. Their answer was to split it according to each player's chance of winning from the current position, which meant putting a number on an outcome that had not happened. That is the foundation of insurance premiums, option prices and expected value.
Who was John Graunt and what did he publish in 1662?

Graunt was a London shopkeeper who sold buttons and ribbons. In 1662 he analysed the parish Bills of Mortality and produced the first serious table of life expectancy. He also showed that you could learn reliably about a whole population from a sample of it, which founded both demography and statistical sampling.
What is the difference between risk and uncertainty as Frank Knight defined it in 1921?

Risk is an unknown whose possibilities you can enumerate and whose odds you can estimate, like fire in a large city. Uncertainty is an unknown with no reliable precedent, like a genuinely new technology or panic. Keynes made the same distinction the same year in A Treatise on Probability.
What did Daniel Bernoulli add in 1738 with the Saint Petersburg paradox?

He showed that a gamble with an infinite mathematical expectation attracts only a modest stake in practice. His explanation was utility: people value what money does for them, not the money itself, so each extra pound is worth less than the last. Risk therefore depends on who is bearing it.
What was Francis Galton's finding about sweet peas in 1875?

Measuring the seeds of parent plants and their offspring, Galton found that the offspring of extreme parents were less extreme than their parents, drifting back towards the average. He called it regression. It applies to heights, to test scores and to investment returns, though it says nothing about when the pull back will occur.
recap:
Peter Bernstein was ten years old in 1929 when his father sold the family leather factory, put the proceeds into the stock market and lost almost all of it in October. Nobody had been reckless. The lesson sat with him for eighty years: a sensible decision and a ruinous outcome can be the same decision.

He read economics at Harvard, joined the research staff of the New York Federal Reserve in 1941, and spent the war as an intelligence officer in London, where he learned to keep thinking while frightened. In 1951 he took over his late father's investment firm, and spent the next four decades handling other people's uncertainty for a living. In 1974, in the worst bear market since the war, he founded the Journal of Portfolio Management to carry academic risk research to the people actually losing money.

The book he wrote in his seventies asks why humanity took so long to learn to measure the future. His answer is that four things had to be invented. First, notation: Fibonacci brought Hindu Arabic numerals to European commerce in 1202, and you cannot calculate an expectation in Roman numerals. Second, the idea itself: in 1654 Pascal and Fermat, answering a gambler's question about an unfinished game, worked out how to attach a value today to an outcome that has not happened. Third, data: John Graunt counted London's dead in 1662 and Edmond Halley turned Breslau's registers into a mortality table in 1693, which made insurance and annuities honest trades. Fourth, the human element: Daniel Bernoulli showed in 1738 that the same bet means different things to different people, and Galton showed that extremes regress towards the average.

The twentieth century built magnificent machinery on those foundations, from Markowitz's portfolio mathematics in 1952 to the option pricing formula of 1973. But in 1921 both Frank Knight and John Maynard Keynes had warned that measurable risk is not the same as genuine uncertainty, and Bernstein ends his book agreeing with them. Every model assumes the future will scatter like the past. He lived to see that assumption break in 1998 and again in 2008, and he kept saying, right to the end, that we simply do not know what the future holds.

So the question to carry out of this is not what will happen. It is the one he asked for forty years: what are the consequences if I am wrong?
stories: In 1654 a French nobleman and gambler called the Chevalier de Mere asked Blaise Pascal a question that had sat unanswered for a hundred and sixty years. Two players stop a game of chance partway through. How should the pot be divided? Pascal wrote to Pierre de Fermat in Toulouse, and over a short series of letters the two men worked it out. The answer, that you split the stake by each player's chance of winning from where the game stands, is the birth certificate of probability. Here is Daniel Bernoulli's puzzle from 1738. I toss a coin until it comes up heads. If that happens on the first toss I pay you two pounds, on the second four, on the third eight, and so on, doubling each time. Work out the mathematical expectation and it is infinite, so in theory you should hand over everything you own for a ticket. Ask anyone at the table what they would actually pay and you will hear about twenty pounds. Bernoulli's explanation founded modern economics: we do not value money, we value what money does for us.
